analysis.one_liner: Cuts federal environmental reviews to two years, bars climate analysis, and makes it much harder to sue over projects.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Senator Mike Lee with two Republican cosponsors on October 26, 2020, referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, and died there without a hearing or vote when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the National Environmental Policy Act, the 1969 law requiring federal agencies to study the environmental effects of projects they approve, such as highways, pipelines, and mines. It would set a two-year deadline for completing reviews, fine agencies that miss deadlines, ban agencies from considering a project's effect on climate change, and let project sponsors' paid consultants prepare environmental documents. It would also make it much harder for ordinary people to challenge a project in court by tightening who has standing, shortening filing deadlines, and raising the bar for blocking a project with an injunction.
analysis.who_benefits: Project sponsors — especially fossil fuel, mining, and large infrastructure developers — gain faster approvals, shorter and fewer environmental documents, decisions that ignore climate effects, and permits that are automatically approved if the agency does not act within 90 days. Environmental consulting firms gain a new role writing documents for sponsors. States gain the option to take over federal environmental review responsibilities.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Developers, fossil fuel and mining project sponsors

how_it_helps.text: Agencies would have to finish the NEPA process within two years and an environmental impact statement within one year, with the agency's own office budget docked 0.5% for every missed deadline determination [S3].
If an agency does not issue or deny a permit within 90 days, the permit is considered approved [S3].

Agencies could no longer consider whether a proposed action or its alternatives affect climate change, or the effects of greenhouse gas emissions, and could not consider alternatives the project sponsor finds economically infeasible [S3].
Project sponsors could hire a qualified third-party consultant, at their own expense, to prepare the environmental impact statement or assessment that the agency then adopts [S3].

Only plaintiffs who allege direct, tangible personal harm could sue under NEPA, suits must be filed within 150 days of final action, and courts could grant injunctions only on clear and convincing evidence [S3].

The bill would repeal Clean Air Act section 309, which gives the EPA a formal role commenting on environmental impact statements, and bar any reissuance of federal guidance on weighing greenhouse gases in NEPA reviews without an act of Congress [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Communities near federally approved projects would bear unexamined environmental and health effects, and would have a harder time getting court review. Agency budgets would shrink through the penalty mechanism, and the public's formal window to weigh in on major projects would shrink with one-document limits and reused or sponsor-prepared analyses.
analysis.who_pays_short: Communities near projects and agency budgets

drawbacks.text: Banning consideration of climate change and greenhouse gas effects means agencies approving major infrastructure would do so blind to the emissions consequences, and the costs would fall on the public rather than the project sponsor [S3].

The standing limits, 150-day filing window, and clear-and-convincing standard for injunctions would make it far harder for nearby residents and community groups to challenge a project whose review was rushed or flawed [S3].

Allowing sponsor-paid third parties to draft the key environmental document, and deeming permits approved when agencies miss the 90-day deadline, creates pressure toward approvals even where review is incomplete [S3].
Even an honest supporter would acknowledge that the budget penalties could force agencies to produce shallow, rushed analysis of complex projects rather than better ones [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Permitting delays for major projects are real, and parts of the bill — firm deadlines, a single consolidated document, letting states take over reviews with audits and safeguards — address a genuine problem. But the bill goes well beyond streamlining: it removes climate change from agency consideration outright, lets project sponsors' own consultants write the environmental analysis, cuts the EPA's formal role, and raises the bar for courts to halt a flawed project. The savings in time would come largely at the expense of affected communities' information and legal recourse.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in late October 2020 and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Mike Lee introduced the UNSHACKLE Act on October 26, 2020, with Senators Kevin Cramer and Ted Cruz as cosponsors [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day it was introduced [S5].
The committee took no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — and the bill expired when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Communities near federally approved projects kept the existing environmental review process and their ability to challenge it in court. Project sponsors and developers who wanted faster approvals and climate-blind decisions are worse off because it did not pass.

for.name: Mike Lee
for.what_they_did: Introduced the UNSHACKLE Act in the Senate on October 26, 2020.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Never held a hearing or markup and never reported the bill; it sat in committee until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All three sponsors were Republicans, and neither of the cosponsors was a Democrat; no Democratic support appears anywhere in the record.

industries.industry: Fossil fuel and mining project sponsors
industries.note: The bill would speed approvals of pipelines, mines, and drilling-related projects, ban agencies from weighing climate effects, and automatically approve permits agencies fail to act on in 90 days. The time saved comes out of environmental review that protects nearby residents.

Faster reviews and consolidated documents would speed highways, transit, and other projects the public may want. But the shortcuts — climate-blind analysis, sponsor-chosen consultants, restricted standing to sue — fall hardest on the communities hosting the projects.

The bill creates a new channel allowing project sponsors to hire their own consultants to draft the environmental impact statements agencies adopt, with agency oversight. That makes sponsor-funded consultants a permanent part of producing the analysis meant to check the sponsor's project.

The bill restricts who can sue under NEPA, imposes a 150-day filing deadline, raises the evidence standard for injunctions, and limits attorney fee recovery in environmental cases, sharply narrowing the main legal tool citizens have to challenge federal project approvals.
